title: The Winning Test

scenario.situation: A new paywall variant has been running for three days. It shows a 6% lift in subscription conversions and has crossed p<0.05. The PM is ready to ship.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The PM believes the variant is a clear winner and that waiting longer wastes revenue on an inferior control.
scenario.question: Should you call this test and ship the variant?

decisions.prompt: The PM wants a green light. How do you frame your investigation before touching the results?

options.label: Confirm the lift is statistically significant
options.detail: Re-run the significance test yourself to verify the PM's p<0.05 claim.
options.consequence: You confirm p<0.05 — and stop there. But verifying the PM's conclusion with the same test doesn't catch any of the structural problems that could be manufacturing this signal. You've added a step without adding insight.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the stakeholder's conclusion and treated significance as the finish line, not the starting line.

options.label: Run a test-health diagnostic before reading the results
options.detail: Check sample ratio, traffic composition, elapsed vs. planned duration, and whether results were observed early — before interpreting the lift.
options.consequence: You find three problems before even looking at lift: the sample split is off, bot traffic is elevated in one arm, and the test is at 30% of its pre-registered runtime. The 6% signal now has obvious alternative explanations to investigate.

options.label: Segment the result by user cohort
options.detail: Break out conversion lift by new vs. returning users to see which segment is driving the 6%.
options.consequence: Segmentation is useful — but done before checking test health, you're analyzing a potentially contaminated result. Any segment-level finding inherits the same structural problems.
options.divergenceCost: Skipped test-validity checks and began interpreting a result that may be structurally unsound.

options.label: Estimate revenue impact and ship if it's large enough
options.detail: Project the 6% lift to annual revenue; if the number is big, the business case overrides statistical caution.
options.consequence: A large projected number accelerates the decision — but projecting a lift that may be a false positive just scales the error. Revenue framing bypasses the analytical question entirely.
options.divergenceCost: Substituted a business-impact projection for a validity check, compounding the risk of a false winner.

decisions.prompt: Your diagnostic flags two issues: a possible sample-ratio mismatch and early stopping. Which view of the data do you trust to assess what's actually happening?

artifact.title: Observed conversion lift by day — Control vs. Variant
artifact.caption: Raw daily lift percentages. The lift is declining each day and the test is at 30% of its planned duration — but p<0.05 was crossed on Day 3.

options.label: The current p-value and observed lift
options.detail: Use the live significance result: p=0.043, lift=6.1%.
options.consequence: p<0.05 is real — but it was computed on day 3 of a 10-day pre-registered test. Checking significance repeatedly and stopping the moment it crosses is exactly how false positives are manufactured. The p-value is valid only at the pre-registered sample size.
options.divergenceCost: Treated a mid-test p-value as a terminal result, ignoring that repeated peeking inflates the false-positive rate.

options.label: Sample-ratio check + lift trend at full pre-registered duration
options.detail: Verify that control and variant received their intended traffic share; then model the lift trajectory through the planned end date.
options.consequence: The sample ratio is 52/48 instead of 50/50 — a statistically significant mismatch (p=0.01) pointing to bot inflation in the variant arm. Projecting the declining lift trend to day 10 puts the confidence interval squarely overlapping zero. There is no detectable winner.

artifact.title: Sample-ratio check + lift at pre-registered horizon
artifact.caption: Variant arm is over-allocated by 2.3 points — a significant sample-ratio mismatch. Projected lift at the pre-registered horizon is 0.4%, indistinguishable from zero.

decisions.prompt: The sample-ratio mismatch and declining lift trend undercut the early result. What do you tell the PM?

options.label: "The test is invalid — bot traffic broke it. Don't ship."
options.detail: Make the call: declare the test void and stop the conversation.
options.consequence: You're probably right, but 'don't ship' without a path forward leaves the PM with nothing actionable and invites them to override you. Declaring invalidity without a remediation plan isn't an analytical recommendation — it's a veto.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a definitive conclusion and skipped the remediation path, reducing credibility and leaving no forward plan.

options.label: "Early results look promising but two validity problems prevent a clean call — here's how we get a trustworthy answer."
options.detail: Present the SRM finding and peeking risk; recommend bot-traffic filtering, resetting the test, and running to the pre-registered 10-day horizon before deciding.
options.consequence: The PM understands why the current signal can't be trusted, sees a concrete path to a real answer, and the business doesn't ship a potentially null change. You've added rigor without blocking progress.

insight: The 6% lift was a mirage assembled from three compounding errors: repeated significance peeking (which inflates false positives each time you look), a sample-ratio mismatch from bot traffic that over-allocated users to the variant, and a novelty effect that faded by day three. When the test was projected to its pre-registered 10-day horizon with clean traffic, the lift collapsed to near zero. The lesson is that a p-value is only valid at the sample size for which it was pre-registered — stopping the moment significance appears is not optional discipline, it is the entire mechanism that keeps A/B testing honest.
